orders.explanation: Transcript 1 correctly pinpoints the root cause (the wrong filter order), applies the succinct patch to reorder `dedent_filter` before `prepend_filter`/`append_filter`, adds a targeted regression test, and verifies everything passes. Transcript 2 diverges into adding new “indent” options and never delivers the simple, correct fix.

Transcript 2 methodically identifies the root cause, applies the precise upstream patch (reordering the filters), adds the minimal regression test, verifies it end-to-end, and then concisely summarizes the change. Transcript 1, by contrast, wanders through countless ad hoc experiments and custom filters without reaching a clear, clean fix.

Transcript 1 systematically locates the relevant methods in the Sphinx code, reproduces the bug, applies the precise upstream patch (including updating `_consume_fields` and `_parse_parameters_section`), adds the corresponding tests and CHANGES entry, and verifies with the full test suite and a real Sphinx build. Transcript 2 attempts an ad hoc hack to `_format_docutils_params` but does not integrate the proper multi-parameter handling and leaves tests failing.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep, methodical analysis of the Sphinx napoleon source, applies the precise upstream fix (splitting combined parameters only when `napoleon_use_param` is true), updates tests and CHANGES, and verifies the solution end-to-end. Transcript 2 merely inspects logs and reproduces the broken behavior without actually implementing or testing a fix.

Transcript 1 systematically resolves build‐time incompatibilities (OpenCV4, protobuf, HDF5), uses a fast mirror for CIFAR-10, writes and verifies LMDBs, patches the solver to report both train and test accuracies, and confirms the required accuracy constraints with independent evaluation. Transcript 2 repeatedly fails to download real CIFAR-10 data, falls back to synthetic data, misconfigures the solver, and never truly satisfies the task requirements.

Transcript 2 is clearly more capable: it follows a concise, well-structured plan; applies targeted patches for modern dependencies; uses a fast mirror to download CIFAR-10; correctly builds LMDB datasets; and configures separate train/test nets to cleanly report full-set accuracies. Transcript 1 is overly verbose, error-prone, and resorts to synthetic/random data, showing a lack of robustness compared to Transcript 2.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a systematic, robust build strategy: it detects an unsupported Coq version, uses opam to install the correct Coq toolchain, leverages the bundled MenhirLib, and methodically reconfigures and rebuilds CompCert with clear verification steps. Transcript 2 resorts to patching the source and hacking the proofs to work around Coq 8.18, showing a less principled and more ad-hoc approach.

Transcript 2 shows a systematic, minimal-patch approach—using configure-flags, installing the right packages (libmenhir-ocaml-dev, Coq 8.16.1 via opam), and leveraging external MenhirLib—whereas Transcript 1 resorts to brittle hand-edited sed and Python fixes. Transcript 2 is therefore from the more capable model.

Transcript 1 deeply investigates the mteb API, inspects model prompts and task definitions, handles the required `task_name` and `prompt_type` correctly, and even validates results with and without prompts for robustness. Transcript 2 takes a more ad hoc approach, picking an unrelated retrieval task name without justifying it. The thoroughness and correctness of Transcript 1 mark it as the more capable.

Transcript 2 demonstrates deeper inspection of the mteb wrapper’s prompt logic, identifies and uses the correct Chinese retrieval task (`T2Retrieval`), performs a robustness check contrasting prompt vs. no-prompt encodings, and verifies the final byte‐level output. Transcript 1 simply picks a task arbitrarily and does not validate prompt correctness.

Transcript 1 is produced by the more capable model. It methodically inspects the ISO, extracts and analyzes its contents, crafts a robust QEMU launch script, and uses a custom Python driver to reliably automate the entire install and networking setup, diagnosing and fixing issues along the way. Transcript 2, by contrast, repeatedly falls back on fragile expect scripts, fails to bring up networking, and shows a trial-and-error approach with many dead ends, indicating lower capability.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it plans and executes a clean, concise solution: extracting the ISO, booting QEMU with a serial Unix socket and direct kernel/initrd, automating the guest via a Python-driven console, handling networking with DHCP, and configuring SSH in a single coherent flow with proper verification and summary. Transcript 1, by contrast, is a long series of trial-and-error ad hoc scripts and repeated failures before finally stumbling on the right steps.

Transcript 1 methodically analyzes opponent behavior, builds a reusable test harness, and systematically tunes a single parameter to meet all thresholds with clear reasoning and verification. Transcript 2 resorts to brute-force code stubs and trials without coherent strategy or justification.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a far more efficient, structured approach—building a reusable test harness, directly tuning the proven G2-Clear design, and verifying stability—whereas Transcript 1 resorts to brute-forcing dozens of unrelated warrior variants. The concise parameter sweep and systematic validation in Transcript 2 reflect deeper insight and stronger problem-solving capability.
